newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH ELECTION VIEW - FINANCIAL ANALYSTS COMMENT.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH ELECTION VIEW - FINANCIAL ANALYSTS COMMENT.

text.p: Following are comments from analysts in the financial markets after a runoff vote in France's parliamentary election pointing to a victory for the left.
DARREN WILLIAMS, INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIST, UBS, LONDON:

If the polls are right the market can take some comfort from the fact that the Socialists look like they're in on their own but it still raises questions regardless of whether the Communist Party is in government or not.
I'm not sure on European monetary union whether the Socialists are any worse than (Philippe) Seguin (seen as a could-be centre-right prime minister if the right had won).
There's a terrific amount of uncertainty on how the co-habitation (between left government and conservative President Jacques Chirac) is going to pan out.
France has been buffetted for some time now by fiscal and EMU questions. They're in for it again just when they didn't need it.
ERIC CHANEY, ECONOMIST, MORGAN STANLEY, PARIS:

What is interesting is that the Socialists could have majority alone which is not so bad for markets. They would be less prone to be influenced by the Communists on both economic and European policies.
GARY DUGAN, EQUITIES STRATEGIST, JP MORGAN, LONDON:
This is better than the worst outcome, which would have been a heavy reliance on the Communists for an absolute majority.
Most people had given up on a victory by the right, but even so, I still see the markets down or flat.
Until we get an absolutely clear indication on France Telecom, I see privatisation stocks and restructuring stories continuing to underperform.
ELISABETTA CASTELLI, HEAD INT'L EQUITIES, CDC BOURSE, PARIS:
Although the uncertainty has been taken away on the election result, we really do not know what the programme is.

What we've heard is of concern to the financial markets. We don't know whether France Telecom and Thomson-CSF will be privatised. How are they going to get the budget deficit down? Will they delay entry into the Euro?
We will be waiting on the lips of the politicians. There will be considerable volatility as announcements come through on policy decisions.
PHILIPPE BROSSARD, HEAD OF RESEARCH, ABN AMRO, PARIS:
"It looks like the Socialists have an absolute majority, so the market reaction may be rather soft -- I would still say slightly negative but maybe not all that much.
DOMINIQUE BARBET, ECONOMIST, PARIBAS, PARIS:

"If there's an absolute Socialist majority, I don't think there'll be a big market fall. We'll see how this election evening turns out, the declarations from the various sides, but a priori the markets should feel more at ease with the idea that an alliance with the Communists is not indispensable.
Nonetheless the majority will be slim.

I think the market reaction will obviously not be positive but the victory is clear and the fall in markets should be relatively limited, especially if the Socialists absolute majority alone is confirmed.
It (the fall) will perhaps be a bit stronger on the stock market than on PIBOR (interest rate futures).
